newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK - CPI, other data week's focus.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK - CPI, other data week's focus.

text.p: Traders of U.S. government securities expect to have a busy week on their hands following Friday's bloodbath in the bond market.
Several important economic releases scheduled include U.S. consumer prices Tuesday, business inventories Wednesday and industrial production and capacity utilization Friday.

"The big number we'll see next week is CPI and we think it will rise in line with recent increases, that is 0.3 percent overall and 0.2 in the core rate," said David Jones, chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co.
Market participants were still reeling late Friday after a far stronger-than-anticipated reading on U.S. jobs creation sent the U.S. Treasury market into a tailspin.
The strong jobs report led many Wall Street analysts to revise their forecasts on the strength of the economy. It also ignited fears that the Federal Reserve may move

sooner-than-anticipated to stanch growth by tightening monetary policy. Some market participants believe that the risk of a tightening could come at the next meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee's meeting on February 4 and 5.

Jones still maintained, however, that the Fed would not move to tighten at its February meeting. "My sense is Greenspan and the policymakers will have to see the whites of inflation's eyes in their face before they move," he said. Jones said the one area the solid jobs gains could affect
the most is industrial production and capacity utilization.

"Manufacturing employment was up a sharp 0.9 percent in November as a result of the General Motors strike being resolved and also up sharply in December (19,000)," Jones said. "Overtime levels were higher and this all points to strain in that sector." Regional surveys from the Atlanta and Richmond Federal Reserve Banks will be released on Tuesday and the Philadelphia Fed on Thursday. "The Philly Fed survey is never a market mover," said Lanston's Jones.
In addition, U.S. retail sales data are slated for release on Tuesday. International trade and the preliminary University of Michigan January consumer confidence are scheduled for Friday.
Economists surveyed by Reuters showed they expected an overall CPI reading of plus 0.3 percent, same as last month's. The core rate also was seen unchanged, up 0.2 percent.

Analysts surveyed by Reuters also saw retail sales picking up sharply, from a negative 0.4 percent in the previous report to a positive 0.5 percent. Excluding autos, sales should rise slightly from 0.3 percent to 0.4 percent, the poll showed.

Reuters' poll also showed business inventories were expected to dip to a positive 0.3 percent from a positive 0.5 percent. The U.S. international trade deficit was seen increasing to $9.8 billion from $7.99 billion.
The polls also showed expectations that U.S. industrial production would post another healthy gain, up 0.6 percent from the previous reading of a 0.9 percent increase.
In late trading Friday the 30-year bond was down 1-5/32 at 95-20/32 to yield 6.84 percent.

The two-year note was at 99-14/32 to yield 6.06 percent, down 7/32. The five-year note was down 17/32 at 98-29/32 to yield 6.38 percent, while the 10-year note was at 99-6/32, down 26/32, to yield 6.61 percent.
Federal funds closed at 5-3/16 percent, near the Federal Reserve's current target level and were expected to open trade Monday at between 5.25 percent and 5 5/16 percent.
